analysis.one_liner: Caps yearly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $2,000 in ACA marketplace plans.
analysis.headline: A single House member introduced a bill to cap annual out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,000 for people in ACA marketplace plans; it sits in committee with zero cosponsors and no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Affordable Care Act so that people buying health plans on the ACA marketplaces could pay no more than $2,000 a year out of their own pockets for prescription drugs ($4,000 for family coverage), starting in 2027, with the cap rising with medical costs after that. It borrows an idea Congress already applied to Medicare drug plans, where a $2,000 drug cost cap took effect in 2025, and extends the same kind of protection to marketplace coverage. Today, marketplace plans can require patients to pay thousands of dollars toward expensive drugs before their overall out-of-pocket maximum is reached.
analysis.who_benefits: Marketplace plan enrollees who take expensive prescription drugs — especially people on costly specialty drugs for cancer, multiple sclerosis, HIV, or autoimmune conditions — who would stop paying for those drugs once they hit $2,000 in a year.

how_it_helps.text: Caps annual prescription drug cost-sharing at $2,000 for self-only marketplace coverage and $4,000 for other coverage, for plan years starting in 2027, with the cap indexed to rise with the premium adjustment percentage in later years [S2].

Once an enrollee has paid $2,000 toward drugs, the plan must cover prescription drug benefits without further cost-sharing counting against them, under the bill's conforming amendments to the ACA and the Public Health Service Act [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers offering marketplace plans would absorb the drug costs above the cap, and would likely shift much of that added cost into premiums paid by all marketplace enrollees. Brand-name drug makers keep selling at current prices, now with fewer patients priced out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Marketplace insurers and all enrollees' premiums

drawbacks.text: A targeted cap raises plans' costs, and insurers generally offset that by raising premiums for everyone in the marketplace, so enrollees who take no drugs would pay more through premiums — a standard trade-off of any benefit mandate [S2].

The cap applies only to ACA marketplace plans; people with employer coverage, Medicare beneficiaries (who already have a $2,000 drug cap under a separate law), and the uninsured get nothing from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: no one on a marketplace plan should be paying many thousands of dollars a year just to stay on their medication, and a hard $2,000 cap delivers that. The honest cost is that the burden moves rather than disappears — insurers pay more, and premiums for all marketplace shoppers likely rise to cover it, which hits middle-income enrollees who get little or no subsidy. Whether the trade is worth it depends on how large that premium spread ends up being.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss introduced the bill on November 20, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action has been taken since [S4].
No other member has cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet — the bill is parked in committee. Marketplace patients on costly drugs are still paying full drug cost-sharing, and insurers and drug makers face no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill is parked in committee

for.name: Rep. Jake Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote or cosponsor record yet — the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.industry: Health insurers offering ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: The bill forces them to cover drug costs above $2,000 per patient, a direct hit to their cost structure; they can recoup it by raising premiums for all enrollees. Their financial interest runs against the cap, though the added cost ultimately flows back to the same patients the bill helps.

The bill does nothing to lower drug list prices; it only shifts who pays. Patients who currently skip or ration expensive prescriptions because of cost-sharing would be able to fill them, at the insurer's expense — more volume at today's prices. Cheaper access for patients, but the underlying prices stay high.

analysis.trajectory: This is a one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors, referred to a committee that has not acted on it. The overwhelming pattern for private members' health bills at this stage is that they never get a hearing or a floor vote. It could gain traction only if it attracts cosponsors and leadership decides to move it, which is unlikely this session unless drug pricing becomes a priority.
